In the college library's reading room, Mohit slid his phone across the table to Chetan. "Look. Proof that the new metro line will flood the whole east side. Share it before the council vote."
Chetan read it. A dramatic photo, a lot of capital letters, no author, no date.
"Where's this from?"
"Doesn't matter, it's everywhere."
"That's exactly why it matters." Chetan searched the photo. It was from a flood in another country, four years ago.
Mohit's face went red. "Okay, but the other side lies too."
"Maybe. So let's read both." Chetan pulled up the city's engineering report and a residents' group's objections. They spent an hour on it. The flooding risk was real in one area, and the report admitted it. The viral post was still fake.

qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit defensive; his face went red and he said the other side lies too.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that helped them judge the issue fairly?
qa.a: He checked the photo's source and then read both the city report and the residents' objections before deciding.

Dear Vasudha,
You asked why I stopped forwarding those videos in our family group. Here's why.
In my media course we did an exercise: take one video you believe and one you hate, and check both the same way. Who made it, who paid, what's cut out, what music they use to make you feel something.
I picked a clip about our state that made me furious. It had sad music, a crying woman and no dates. Then I checked one from the other side. Same tricks, different villain.
I felt a bit foolish and honestly shaken. I'd been angry on cue.
Now I pause when a video makes me feel something fast. I still have opinions. I just want them to be mine.
Love,
Gurleen

qa.a: Sad music, a crying woman and no dates.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after checking both videos?
qa.a: Gurleen felt foolish and shaken, realising the anger had been triggered on cue.

qa.q: What habit is Gurleen building, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Pausing when a video stirs a fast feeling, and checking who made it and what is cut, so opinions are based on facts.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vasudha may feel curious and perhaps a little challenged, especially if Vasudha also forwards such videos.

Ganga, you're recording? Fine. My name is Lakshmi, and I used to be the family's news source. Every morning I'd forward three things to our aunties' group.
Then, in my second year of college, I forwarded a post saying a local temple trust was stealing donations. It turned out to be completely made up by someone fighting an election. My Periamma, who volunteers there, cried on the phone.
I felt terrible. I apologised to everyone in the group.
After that I set myself a rule: if a post makes me angry fast, wait a day, find the original source, and read one sensible person from the other side. It's slow. It's boring. It's saved me from forwarding at least ten lies.
Now the aunties call me before they forward.

"The rent's going up by a lot," said Ramesh, the landlord, standing in the doorway of Noor's rented room.
Noor took a breath. "I understand prices went up. Can we talk about it?"
"What's to talk about?"
"I've paid on time for two years. I fixed the tap myself last month. And you won't need to find a new tenant or paint the room."
Ramesh folded his arms. "Everyone says they're a good tenant."
"True. So how about a smaller increase now, and we look at it again next year? And I'll sign for a full year."
He thought about it. "A full year?"
"A full year."
"Half the increase, then. And you keep fixing the tap."
Noor laughed. "Deal."
When the door shut, her hands were trembling, but she was smiling.

My first job offer came with a salary lower than my classmates got. I'm Thomas, and I almost accepted it on the spot because I was scared they'd take it back.
My friend Ishita, who'd done this before, said, "Ask. Politely. The worst they say is no."
I spent a night preparing. I wrote what I'd bring: the internship project, two languages, willingness to travel. I practised saying the number out loud until it stopped sounding rude.
On the call, my voice shook. I said I was excited to join and asked if there was room on the salary. The HR manager said the salary was fixed, but she could offer an earlier review and a laptop allowance.
I took it. Not everything I wanted. More than I'd have got by staying silent.

Vasudha and Ojas were assigned to present one joint design to a local shop owner. They each wanted their own concept. By Tuesday they weren't speaking.

On the last evening before college, Noor sat on the roof of her family's house in their small town, looking at the mustard fields turning dark.
Tomorrow the bus would take her to the city. She had dreamt of it for years: libraries, a hostel room, being someone new.
Her little brother Kamal climbed up and sat beside her. "You're happy, right?"
"So happy," she said, and her voice cracked.
Kamal frowned. "Then why are you crying?"
Noor laughed through it. "Because I'll miss the fields. And you. And Ammi's burnt rotis. And I really, really want to go."
Kamal thought hard. "Can you want two things?"
"Apparently."
He leaned his head on her shoulder. They watched the last light go.

qa.q: Where did Noor sit on the last evening?
qa.a: On the roof of her family's house.

qa.q: What does Noor's cracking voice suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she feels both deeply excited and sad, wanting to go while missing home already.

qa.q: How could Noor's family support her through this mix of feelings?
qa.a: They could let her talk about both sides, plan calls or visits, and not treat her tears as doubt about going.

qa.q: How does Kamal see his sister leaving?
qa.a: Kamal is confused that someone happy could cry, then accepts it and stays close to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding excitement and grief about leaving home at once.

Hana had waited three years to move out of her parents' flat in Osaka. Now she stood in her own tiny apartment, boxes everywhere, the silence enormous.
Her friend Nour, who'd helped carry the boxes, flopped onto the floor. "So? Freedom!"
"Freedom," Hana repeated. She opened the fridge. Empty. She hadn't thought about groceries. Or the gas bill. Or how quiet it would be at night.
"You look terrified," Nour said.
"I'm thrilled," Hana said. "And terrified. And I want to call my mum and also never call her so she doesn't know I'm scared."
Nour laughed. "Call her. Tell her you're thrilled. Tell her you need her curry recipe."
Hana sat down on a box and laughed too, which almost turned into crying.

qa.q: How long had Hana waited to move out?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: How does Hana feel standing in her new apartment?
qa.a: She feels thrilled and terrified at once, torn between wanting to call her mum and hiding her fear.

qa.a: Calling her mum and asking for a recipe, which lets Hana stay connected without giving up her new independence.

qa.q: What is it like for Nour to watch Hana on moving day?

The swing was still there, its chain rusted. The mango tree they used to climb had been cut down. The classroom walls had been painted a bright new blue.

"You look like someone died," Yash said.

Yash sat on the step. "You hated school."

Kwame's first job in Accra meant long hours and a small rented room. On Sunday he went back to his childhood neighbourhood to see his old friend Rafael.
They bought roasted plantain from the same corner woman, who now had grey hair. "You boys used to steal from me," she said, and gave them extra.

They stayed and watched the game till the streetlights came on.

The month my father got sick, everything landed on me at once. I'm Aparna, the older daughter, twenty-one, three months into my first job.
Suddenly I was the one talking to doctors, paying the electricity bill, filling his insurance claim, and answering my younger brother's school emails. I'd sit at my laptop at midnight and stare, not typing anything. I'd forget to eat.

We made a list. We split it into this week, this month, later. I called my aunt for help with the hospital.
I still get flooded. But now I know where to start.

passage:
When my knee injury ended my chance at the state football team, I spent a year fighting it. I'm Hansa, and I went to three physios, watched recovery videos at night, and ran on it too early.
My friend Ritu came to every appointment. After the third doctor said the same thing, she asked me gently, "What would happen if you stopped fighting this?"
I wanted to scream at her. Instead I cried on the hospital steps.
Something shifted after that. I stopped asking "why me" and started asking "what now." I began coaching the under-12 girls at our club. I still ache watching matches. But I laugh more at practice than I did in my last season playing.

qa.q: How many physios did Hansa go to?
qa.a: Three physios.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when Ritu asked her question?
qa.a: Hansa felt angry and then heartbroken, wanting to scream and crying on the hospital steps.

qa.q: What helped Hansa begin to accept the injury?
qa.a: Ritu's gentle question and Hansa's shift from "why me" to "what now", which led to coaching.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt going to every appointment?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt worried and patient, hoping her friend would find a way forward.

grounding: A young adult reflects on accepting the end of a sporting dream and adapting.

passage:
Warden's note, graduate hostel
Bhupen came to the office after his family told him they were selling the house he grew up in. He had been trying to stop the sale for weeks, calling relatives and arguing with his father.
Salma, his friend from the next room, said he had not been sleeping.
When we spoke, he said, "It's already sold. I keep fighting as if I can undo it."
I did not tell him how to feel. I asked what he wanted to keep from the house. He said the neem tree and his mother's kitchen. We talked about taking photos, one last visit, perhaps planting a neem sapling somewhere new.
He left saying he would call his father to plan the visit. I have asked him to see the campus counsellor too.

qa.q: What did Bhupen want to keep from the house?
qa.a: The neem tree and his mother's kitchen.

qa.q: How was Bhupen feeling when he came to the office?
qa.a: He felt grief-stricken and restless, still fighting a sale he knew was done.

qa.q: Which step helped Bhupen move toward acceptance?
qa.a: Asking what he wanted to keep turned his focus from fighting to remembering, with a last visit and a new sapling.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's father feel when Bhupen calls to plan the visit?
qa.a: His father may feel relieved and moved that the arguing has turned into a shared goodbye.

grounding: A warden records a young adult shifting from fighting to accepting the sale of his childhood home.

passage:
Jasleen failed the civil services prelims for the second time. She sat in her small rented room in Delhi and didn't open a book for a week.
Her roommate Seema brought her parathas and left them on her desk without comment.
On the eighth day, Jasleen opened her answer sheets and made herself read every mistake. It hurt. Current affairs had pulled her down both times.
She wrote a new timetable: newspaper at seven, mock tests every Sunday, one full day off a week so she wouldn't burn out. She pinned it above her bed.
Seema read it. "Third time?"
"Third time." Jasleen's voice was steady. "And if not, I'll know I gave it everything."
Seema squeezed her shoulder and went to make chai.

qa.q: What pulled Jasleen down both times?
qa.a: Current affairs.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on the eighth day reading her mistakes?
qa.a: She felt hurt but steady and determined, making herself face every error.

qa.q: What makes Jasleen's new plan likely to help?
qa.a: It targets her weak area, adds regular mock tests, and includes a day off to avoid burning out.

qa.q: How does Seema seem to feel about Jasleen's week of silence?
qa.a: Seema seems concerned but patient, quietly bringing food and then supporting her new plan.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a major setback and committing to try again.

passage:
"You're applying again?" Francis asked, stirring his tea.
"Yes." Lokesh closed the laptop. "Eleven rejections. I'm sending the twelfth."
"Don't you feel stupid?"
"Every time." Lokesh laughed. "But I read all the feedback. Three of them said my portfolio was weak on print design. So I did a print course."
"And if this one says no?"
"Then I'll know something else to fix."
Francis watched him. "Last year you gave up on football after one bad match."
"I know. That's why I'm doing this. I didn't like who I was when I gave up."
"Okay." Francis pushed his cup aside. "Show me the portfolio. I'll tell you what's boring."
"Brutal?"
"Brutal."

qa.q: How many rejections has Lokesh had?
qa.a: Eleven rejections.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's laugh suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels embarrassed by the rejections but determined not to give up.

qa.q: What is Lokesh doing that makes trying again wise?
qa.a: He reads the feedback and fixes the weakness, like taking a print course, before applying again.

qa.q: How is Francis affected by Lokesh's attitude?
qa.a: Francis is surprised, remembering Lokesh quit football, and is moved to help review the portfolio.

grounding: Shows a young adult building grit to keep trying after repeated rejection.

passage:
I failed my nursing licence exam by four marks. I'm Jyoti. I remember reading the result in the hospital canteen and not being able to swallow.
For a week I told everyone I was done. I'd go back to my village, help in my uncle's shop, forget it.
My senior Nirmala didi found me on the stairs during a night shift. She didn't lecture. She said, "I failed twice. Look at me now." She was the ward in-charge.
Something in me got stubborn. I booked the next exam date that night. I studied at five in the morning before shifts, with her old notes.
I passed the second time. I still keep the first result slip in my drawer. It reminds me I can get up.

qa.q: By how many marks did Jyoti fail?
qa.a: Four marks.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel on first reading the result?
qa.a: Jyoti felt crushed and defeated, unable to swallow and saying it was over.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jyoti?
qa.a: Nirmala didi's story of failing twice sparked stubbornness, and Jyoti booked the next exam that night.

qa.q: How might Nirmala didi have felt seeing Jyoti pass?
qa.a: Nirmala didi would likely feel proud and happy that sharing her own failure helped.

grounding: A young adult recalls finding the grit to retake an exam after a painful failure.

passage:
"Dhruv. It's Saturday. Why is your laptop open?" Lalremsiami asked.
"Report due Monday."
"You said that last Saturday. And the one before."
He rubbed his eyes. "I don't remember the last time I did something for fun."
She held up a frisbee. "I do. College. You were terrible at this."
"I was great at this."
"Prove it."
He sighed, shut the laptop and followed her to the park. He dropped the first three throws. Then she tripped over a dog, and they both laughed so hard they had to sit on the grass.
An hour later he opened the laptop again. The report went twice as fast.
"Same time next Saturday?" she said.
"Put it in my calendar. Seriously. Like a meeting."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami hold up?
qa.a: A frisbee.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel before going to the park?
qa.a: He felt tired and a little sad, realising he couldn't remember the last time he had fun.

qa.q: What did the frisbee break do for Dhruv, and how can he keep it?
qa.a: It relaxed him so the report went twice as fast; putting play in his calendar like a meeting can protect it.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel about getting Dhruv outside?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and a bit triumphant, and cares about him not burning out.

grounding: Shows a young adult rediscovering play as a counterweight to work stress.

passage:
Final-year exams, part-time job, a project that wouldn't end. I'm Disha, and last winter I forgot how to laugh.
My flatmate Ira noticed first. "You used to sing in the shower. Now you just shower like a robot."
She dragged me to an open-mic comedy night at a café. I didn't want to go. I sat at the back with my arms crossed. Then a nervous boy did five minutes about his grandmother's forwarded good-morning messages, and I laughed so hard I snorted.
Something unlocked. I started drawing silly cartoons again on Sunday mornings, just for me.
My marks didn't drop. If anything, I focused better. I now think fun isn't a reward for finishing work. It's part of how I keep going.

qa.q: Where did Ira take Disha?
qa.a: To an open-mic comedy night at a café.

qa.q: How was Disha feeling before the comedy night?
qa.a: Disha felt worn out and flat, reluctant to go and sitting with crossed arms.

qa.q: What did Disha learn about balancing work and fun?
qa.a: That play isn't just a reward after work but part of what keeps a person going, so it needs a regular place.

qa.q: How might Ira feel seeing Disha laugh again?
qa.a: Ira would likely feel relieved and happy that her flatmate came back to life a little.

grounding: A young adult reflects on reclaiming playfulness and humour to counter burnout.

passage:
Team lead's note, customer support team
Deepika has been on our team for a year and is one of our most reliable people. In the last two months I noticed she had stopped joining lunch, skipped the Friday quiz, and was answering emails at midnight.
Ojas, who sits next to her, mentioned she seemed flat and irritable.
I spoke to her. She said she felt guilty doing anything that wasn't work. I told her our best work comes from rested people, not exhausted ones, and I asked her to take her full breaks.
The next Friday, she joined the quiz. She got the silliest question wrong and laughed louder than anyone. Ojas says she has started a Tuesday board-game hour.
I will keep an eye on after-hours emails across the team.

qa.q: What did Deepika stop joining?
qa.a: Lunch, and she skipped the Friday quiz.

qa.q: How was Deepika feeling before the team lead spoke to her?
qa.a: She felt flat, irritable and guilty about doing anything that wasn't work.

qa.q: Which step by the team lead helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking her to take full breaks gave her permission to rest, which let her playful side return.

qa.q: How might Ojas see the change in Deepika?
qa.a: Ojas seems glad and relieved, noting she has even started a board-game hour.

grounding: A team lead records a young adult rediscovering play to balance work stress.
